items.prompt: A problem asks for the minimum capacity that makes a schedule feasible. Which candidate domain should binary search operate on?

options.text: Only the indices of input jobs.
An ordered range of possible capacity values.
The two values true and false.
Possible numbers of loop iterations.

feedback.reason: Binary search on answer searches the value being optimized.

blocks.text: Separate input data from candidate answers

The requested output is a capacity, so each searchable candidate must be a possible capacity value. The jobs remain fixed input to feasible(capacity), which simulates or counts whether that candidate can meet the schedule.

items: Name the optimized quantity: minimum feasible capacity.
Derive an ordered integer interval containing every possible optimal capacity.
For a midpoint capacity c, evaluate whether the fixed jobs can be scheduled under c.
Use the proven false-to-true transition to discard capacity values, not job positions.

blocks.title: Recognition rule
blocks.text: If the output is an ordered threshold and a candidate can be classified yes/no monotonically, search the threshold domain even when no input element equals the optimum.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.job_indices: A job index identifies input data but cannot represent a capacity such as the sum required for one schedule period.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.result_booleans: True and false are predicate outputs used to eliminate candidates; they do not encode which numeric capacity is minimal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.loop_counts: The number of iterations follows from the chosen capacity range and is not the quantity requested by the problem.

items.prompt: For minimizing capacity, feasible(x) is false for small x and true for large x. Which result should be returned?

options.text: The last feasible candidate.
The first infeasible candidate.
The first feasible candidate.
Any feasible candidate.

feedback.reason: Minimization over false-to-true feasibility is a first-true boundary problem.

blocks.text: The minimum feasible value is the transition

False-to-true feasibility partitions the ordered domain into capacities that are too small followed by capacities that work. Minimization asks for the boundary's first value, not merely any point in the true suffix.

items: Suppose capacities 1 through 7 yield false, false, false, true, true, true, true.
Capacity 4 is the first true candidate; every smaller value is infeasible and every larger true value is feasible but not minimal.
When feasible(mid) is true, retain mid and search left. When false, discard mid and every smaller candidate.

blocks.title: Objective-to-boundary mapping
blocks.text: Minimize a false-to-true predicate by returning first true. Maximize a true-to-false predicate by returning last true.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.last_true: Once feasibility becomes true for all larger candidates, the last true is merely the high end of the domain and does not minimize capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_false: A false candidate violates the schedule requirement, so it cannot be returned as a feasible minimum.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.any_true: Any true candidate proves existence but may lie strictly after the transition and therefore fail minimality.

items.prompt: For maximizing a minimum distance, valid(d) is true for small d and false for large d. Which result should be returned?

options.text: The first valid distance.
The first invalid distance.
The maximum bound without checking feasibility.
The last valid distance.

feedback.reason: Maximization over a true-to-false predicate is a last-true boundary problem.

blocks.text: The maximum valid value is the final true point

For a minimum-distance requirement, a small distance is easier to satisfy. Once a distance becomes impossible, every larger requirement remains impossible, producing a true prefix followed by a false suffix.

items: If distances 1 through 6 yield true, true, true, false, false, false, the largest achievable requirement is 3.
A true midpoint remains a possible maximum, so retain it and search larger values.
A false midpoint and every larger value can be discarded by the true-to-false proof.

blocks.title: Do not return first false
blocks.text: First false is the exclusive boundary immediately after the valid region. The requested feasible maximum is its predecessor, the last true candidate.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_true: The first true candidate is at the easy low end of the domain and does not maximize the distance requirement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_false: This candidate is already invalid; it can delimit the true prefix but cannot satisfy the requested feasible result.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.domain_max: An enclosing upper bound need not be achievable, so returning it without evaluating validity can exceed the optimum.

items.prompt: Does the optimal answer need to appear as an element of the input array?

options.text: Yes. Binary search can inspect only values stored in the input.
No. It may be any candidate value in the explicitly modeled answer domain.
Yes. Every midpoint is an input index.
It appears in the input only when the input is sorted.

feedback.reason: Answer-space search is distinct from index search.

blocks.text: Midpoint can be a value not stored in the input

Index binary search chooses mid as a position and reads input[mid]. Answer-space search chooses mid as a candidate output value and passes it to a predicate; no input element needs to equal that value.

items: Jobs [3, 5, 6] are input values.
A schedule constraint can make capacity 8 optimal even though 8 is not a job size.
The predicate feasible(8) uses the jobs to evaluate the candidate; binary search narrows the numeric capacity range containing 8.

blocks.title: Input sorting is not the defining requirement
blocks.text: The ordered structure belongs to candidate answers and predicate truth. The predicate may internally use sorted or unsorted input depending on the problem.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_input_only: The search can enumerate an implicit integer range and evaluate each midpoint without finding that value in the input array.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_mid_index: Here mid is an answer value such as capacity or distance, not an index used to access an element.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_if_sorted: Sorting input can help a particular predicate, but it does not force the optimal threshold to equal an input value.

items.prompt: What makes a lower answer bound sound?

options.text: It is a convenient small number.
It always equals the minimum input value.
No valid optimal answer can lie below it.
It is always zero.

feedback.reason: Search bounds must contain every possible optimal answer.

blocks.text: A lower bound needs an impossibility proof below it
A sound lower bound L guarantees optimum >= L. That guarantee can follow from a mandatory individual requirement, a counting or averaging inequality, or an explicit domain constraint.

items: For indivisible jobs, capacity below max(job) cannot process the largest job, so max(job) is a valid lower bound.
Starting above that proven limit can skip the optimum unless another proof excludes the skipped candidates.
Starting lower may remain correct but widens the domain; starting higher without proof is incorrect.

blocks.title: Soundness versus tightness
blocks.text: Sound means the optimum is enclosed. Tight means unnecessary candidates are also excluded. Tightness improves iterations; soundness is required for correctness.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.looks_small: A convenient number can still lie above the true optimum and exclude it; the bound needs a problem-specific proof.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.input_min_always: The minimum input value may be unrelated to the optimized threshold; indivisible capacity, for example, is bounded below by the maximum job.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_always: Some domains forbid zero or have mandatory positive requirements, so zero is not a universally valid or tight lower bound.

items.prompt: What makes an upper answer bound sound?

options.text: It must always equal the largest input value.
Any arbitrarily large number is automatically safe and efficient.
It equals the first midpoint selected.
It is guaranteed to be at or beyond every possible optimum, often with a known feasible candidate for minimization.

feedback.reason: The upper boundary must complete the enclosure of the answer domain.

blocks.text: An upper bound needs an enclosure proof

A sound upper bound U guarantees optimum <= U. For first-feasible minimization whose public contract promises a solution, making U a known feasible candidate also anchors the true side of the false-to-true transition.

items: If one period may process all jobs, sum(jobs) is feasible and no minimum capacity needs to exceed it.
The largest individual job is not always sufficient as an upper bound when multiple jobs must share a period.
An excessively large machine limit may still enclose the answer but can overflow arithmetic and increases log(domain width).

blocks.title: No-solution contracts differ
blocks.text: If the public contract permits no feasible candidate, the search must include and interpret an explicit sentinel instead of assuming the upper endpoint is feasible.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.largest_input_always: The maximum input item may be only a lower bound; combined work or another constraint can require a larger feasible answer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.random_large: An arbitrary machine maximum can overflow sums or midpoint expressions and needlessly widens the logarithmic search domain.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_mid: The midpoint is computed from already justified endpoints, so it cannot supply the proof that those endpoints enclose the optimum.

items.prompt: Why is a feasibility predicate different from the optimization objective?

options.text: They are always the same numeric expression.
The predicate answers whether one candidate works; binary search uses those decisions to locate the optimum boundary.
The predicate must return an input index.
The objective can be ignored once a predicate exists.

feedback.reason: Binary search reduces optimization to repeated decision problems.

blocks.text: The predicate classifies; the boundary optimizes

The optimization objective asks for an extremal value such as minimum capacity. feasible(c) answers the simpler decision question “Does capacity c satisfy every constraint?” for exactly one candidate.

items: Evaluate feasible(mid) to obtain one boolean.
Use monotonicity to extend that boolean to an entire smaller or larger region.
Repeat decisions until the first-true or last-true boundary is isolated.
Return the boundary value as the optimized result.

blocks.title: The objective still controls the search
blocks.text: The same predicate direction can support different questions. The requested minimum or maximum determines which transition boundary and endpoint contract are correct.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_value: The predicate returns a boolean classification for one candidate, while the objective returns an extremal candidate value after many classifications.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.predicate_returns_index: A feasibility oracle normally returns true or false; input positions may be internal data but are not its required output.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.objective_not_needed: Without the objective, the algorithm cannot choose the answer domain, minimization versus maximization, or first-true versus last-true semantics.

items.prompt: A proposed feasibility predicate returns true, false, then true again as capacity increases. What is the correct diagnosis?

options.text: An upper-biased midpoint will repair it.
Running binary search twice guarantees the optimum.
The predicate or candidate model is not suitable for ordinary binary search on answer.
Sorting the boolean results during the search will fix them.

feedback.reason: Answer-space search needs one monotonic feasibility transition.

blocks.text: A repeated truth transition destroys safe elimination

Ordinary binary search needs each predicate result to classify a whole side. A true, false, true pattern has at least two transitions, so a false midpoint does not prove that all larger candidates are false.

items: Suppose candidates 1, 2, 3 yield true, false, true.
Inspecting candidate 2 as false cannot discard candidate 3, because 3 is true.
Any standard update that removes a whole side can therefore remove a valid optimum.
Repair the mathematical candidate model if a monotonic formulation exists; otherwise choose an algorithm that supports multiple valid regions.

blocks.title: Mechanics cannot repair semantics
blocks.text: Midpoint bias solves progress at adjacent boundaries. It cannot turn a nonmonotonic predicate into a one-transition partition.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.use_upper_mid: Upper bias changes which candidate is sampled when two remain, but the sampled boolean still cannot justify discarding a nonmonotonic side.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.search_twice: Repeating an invalid elimination rule offers no guarantee that either run preserves the optimum.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_answers: Predicate truth belongs to fixed candidate values; reordering observed booleans would detach results from candidates and change the problem.

items.prompt: A minimization predicate is true even at the lower bound. What should a correct first-feasible search be able to return?

options.text: Always the upper bound.
The next value after the lower bound.
No answer.
The lower bound itself.

feedback.reason: The search must retain endpoint candidates.

blocks.text: The transition may begin at the first candidate
In false-to-true minimization, feasibility at the declared lower bound means no smaller candidate exists inside the legal domain and the first candidate already satisfies the requirement.

items: Let the domain be [5, 10] and feasible(5) be true.
Monotonicity makes every candidate 5 through 10 true.
The minimum true candidate is therefore 5, the lower endpoint.
A correct true branch retains its midpoint and continues left far enough to preserve that endpoint.

blocks.title: Endpoint test
blocks.text: Test all-feasible and only-upper-feasible domains. Together they expose whether either endpoint is accidentally excluded.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.upper_bound: Every candidate is feasible, so the upper endpoint satisfies the constraint but is not minimal while the lower endpoint exists.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.lower_plus_one: Incrementing the lower endpoint discards a feasible legal candidate that is smaller than every remaining option.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.not_found: A true result at the lower endpoint directly proves that at least one feasible candidate exists.

items.prompt: Which steps are required to model binary search on answer? Select all that apply.

options.text: Define the numeric or ordered quantity being optimized.
Derive sound lower and upper bounds containing the optimum.
Sort the input even when feasibility does not require sorted data.
Define a complete predicate for one candidate.
Prove the predicate changes in one direction.

feedback.reason: Answer-space search is correct only when domain, bounds, predicate, and transition direction are explicit.

blocks.text: Four proofs precede the loop
The implementation is justified only after the optimization problem has been converted into a one-transition boundary problem. Each selected component establishes one part of that conversion.

items: Define the optimized ordered quantity so midpoint values have a clear meaning.
Prove lower and upper bounds enclose every possible optimum and supply any required endpoint feasibility.
Define a complete, stable boolean for one candidate.
Prove how truth changes with the candidate so each boolean safely eliminates one side.

blocks.title: Sorting is predicate-specific
blocks.text: Sort input only when the chosen feasibility check requires ordered data. Candidate monotonicity alone does not imply that the raw input must be sorted.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_input_always: Some predicates scan jobs in original order or use only aggregate values; unconditional sorting adds work and can violate an order-sensitive contract.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.define_answer: Naming capacity, distance, time, or another ordered output creates the candidate domain that the midpoint samples.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.derive_bounds: The search can return the optimum only if every legal optimum lies inside its initial range.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.define_feasibility: Each midpoint needs a reliable decision that includes all constraints for that candidate.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.prove_monotonicity: A one-direction transition is what turns one predicate result into proof that an entire side is impossible.

items.prompt: Which facts can justify answer bounds for minimum processing capacity? Select all that apply.

options.text: Capacity must be at least the largest indivisible job.
The maximum machine integer is always the preferred upper bound.
The total job sum is a safe upper bound when one period may process everything.
Zero is always a valid lower bound regardless of job requirements.

feedback.reason: Bounds should come from problem semantics and known feasible or impossible limits.

blocks.text: Derive both endpoints from the scheduling model

Assume jobs are indivisible and a period may process multiple jobs up to its capacity. Any feasible capacity must fit the largest single job, while capacity equal to the total sum can process all work in one period.

items: For jobs [3, 5, 6], capacity below 6 cannot process the job of size 6, so maxJob = 6 is a sound lower bound.
sumJobs = 14 can process all three jobs in one permitted period, so it is a known feasible upper bound.
The optimum is therefore enclosed in [6, 14].

blocks.title: Do not import bounds without their premise
blocks.text: sumJobs is feasible here only because one period may take everything. A per-period item-count limit or another constraint could invalidate that upper-bound proof.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_without_proof: Positive indivisible jobs cannot fit in zero capacity, so zero ignores the mandatory maxJob lower limit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.random_int_max: A machine maximum is not the preferred semantic bound: it can overflow arithmetic and makes the logarithmic range wider than sumJobs.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.largest_job: Because jobs are indivisible, any capacity below the largest job makes that job impossible to process.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.sum_jobs: Under the stated one-period model, total capacity equal to the sum can process every job together and is therefore feasible.

items.prompt: Which properties must a feasibility predicate satisfy? Select all that apply.

options.text: It fully decides whether the given candidate satisfies the constraints.
It may return an unverified guess when evaluation is expensive.
Increasing candidates preserve truth or falsity in the proven direction.
The same candidate yields the same result during one search.

feedback.reason: The predicate is the correctness oracle for answer-space search.

blocks.text: Every boolean must support irreversible elimination

Binary search never revisits a discarded region. Its predicate must therefore classify the candidate against every stated constraint, produce the same truth for the same search state, and participate in a proven one-direction transition.

items: Complete: true means the candidate really satisfies all requirements, not a subset.
Stable: reevaluating the same candidate during one search cannot contradict an earlier branch.
Monotonic: truth at one candidate proves the required truth or falsity for an entire side.
An unverified approximation can misclassify mid and permanently discard the optimum.

blocks.title: Approximation needs a different contract
blocks.text: Numerical tolerance or probabilistic feasibility can be valid only with an explicit error model and stopping rule; ordinary exact binary-search correctness does not cover an unverified guess.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.approximate_guess: A guessed false or true result can eliminate the side containing the optimum, and ordinary binary search has no recovery mechanism.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.candidate_complete: The branch is sound only if the boolean accounts for every constraint that defines whether the candidate works.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.stable: Previously discarded candidates remain excluded, so the same candidate and unchanged input must not later reverse truth.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.monotonic: A single transition lets one midpoint classification prove that a whole smaller or larger region cannot contain the requested boundary.

items.prompt: Which edge cases should answer-space search handle? Select all that apply.

options.text: The optimum equals the lower bound.
Only a case where the first midpoint is optimal.
No candidate is feasible when the public contract allows a not-found result.
The optimum equals the upper bound.

feedback.reason: Boundary and absent-solution cases validate the full result contract.

blocks.text: Exercise every legal transition location

The predicate transition can occur at either endpoint or, when the public contract permits it, outside the candidate domain. A first-midpoint optimum exercises neither repeated updates nor endpoint retention.

items: Optimum at lower bound: catches a true branch that discards the left endpoint.
Optimum at upper bound: catches a false branch or initialization that excludes the right endpoint.
No feasible candidate: verifies the explicit sentinel or not-found result instead of returning an unverified bound.
Also test two adjacent candidates, because retained-mid updates can stall there.

blocks.title: Contract-dependent absence
blocks.text: Do not add a no-solution sentinel when the problem guarantees a feasible answer; do test it when the public result contract explicitly allows absence.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mid_only: An immediate midpoint success can pass even when branch updates skip endpoints, stall on adjacent values, or mishandle no solution.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.lower_optimum: This proves the smallest legal candidate remains representable through every feasible branch.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.upper_optimum: This proves initialization and infeasible branches can converge on the largest legal candidate.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.none_feasible: When allowed, absence must map to a documented sentinel rather than an arbitrary endpoint.

items.prompt: Arrange a dependency-driven design process for binary search on answer.

elements.text: Define the answer quantity and optimization direction.
Express a complete decision predicate for one candidate of that quantity.
Prove the predicate's transition direction and choose first-true or last-true.
Derive enclosing bounds with the required endpoint status, run the matching boundary search, and verify the optimum.

feedback.reason: The loop is the final step after the optimization problem has been converted into a boundary problem.

blocks.text: Each step supplies the premise for the next
Code-level midpoint and update choices cannot be justified until the output has been modeled as an ordered quantity and one candidate can be classified against the complete requirement.
Dependency chain

items: Define the answer quantity and whether the problem minimizes or maximizes it.
Express a stable, complete predicate that decides whether one candidate value satisfies the constraints.
Prove whether predicate truth is false-to-true or true-to-false, then map minimization or maximization to first true or last true.
Derive bounds that enclose the boundary with the endpoint status the loop assumes, execute the matching search, and verify feasibility plus optimality.

blocks.title: A correct loop cannot rescue a wrong model
blocks.text: If feasibility omits a constraint or truth changes more than once, boundary updates can be mechanically perfect and still discard the real optimum.

items.prompt: Which mechanics belong to a half-open first-feasible search over a false-to-true integer predicate? Select all that apply.

options.text: While left < right, compute a lower-biased midpoint in [left, right).
Return mid immediately whenever feasible(mid) is true.
If feasible, retain mid by moving the right boundary to mid.
If infeasible, move the left boundary to mid + 1.

feedback.reason: A feasible midpoint may be the minimum, while an infeasible midpoint and all smaller candidates are excluded.

blocks.text: Both branches preserve the first feasible boundary
Let x be the first true integer boundary of a false-to-true predicate. A half-open search keeps x between left and right and runs while left < right with a lower-biased midpoint.

items: Lower-biased mid satisfies left <= mid < right, so it is safe to evaluate and the true branch can move right.
If feasible(mid) is true, x <= mid and mid may equal x; right = mid preserves that boundary.
If feasible(mid) is false, monotonicity proves x > mid; left = mid + 1 removes mid and every smaller candidate.
Returning immediately on true would prove feasibility but not that no smaller feasible value exists.

blocks.title: Adjacent candidates
blocks.text: For left = 6 and right = 7, lower mid = 6. True moves right to 6; false moves left to 7. Either result converges without losing the first true boundary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.return_true_mid: A true midpoint may lie after an earlier feasible candidate, so immediate return satisfies feasibility but can violate minimization.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.compute_mid: Lower bias keeps mid below the exclusive right endpoint and guarantees right = mid shrinks the gap.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.keep_feasible: A feasible midpoint can be the first true value, so the true branch must retain it as the right boundary.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.discard_infeasible: False-to-true monotonicity proves an infeasible midpoint and all smaller candidates cannot be the answer.

items.prompt: Which mechanics belong to a progress-safe closed last-valid search over a true-to-false integer predicate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Compute an upper-biased midpoint.
Use a lower-biased midpoint while retaining a valid mid with left = mid.
If valid, set left = mid to search larger candidates.
If invalid, set right = mid - 1.

feedback.reason: A valid midpoint remains a candidate for the maximum and shifts the search right.

blocks.text: Bias toward the side that retains mid

Let x be the last true candidate of a true-to-false predicate, guaranteed to lie in the closed interval [left, right]. The loop runs while left < right and must retain a valid midpoint while seeking a larger one.

items: Upper-biased mid satisfies left < mid <= right when two or more candidates remain.
If valid(mid) is true, x >= mid and mid may equal x; left = mid preserves it and moves the lower boundary.
If valid(mid) is false, x < mid; right = mid - 1 removes mid and every larger candidate.
Lower bias with left = mid can choose mid = left for adjacent candidates and repeat the same interval forever.

blocks.title: Adjacent candidates
blocks.text: For [6, 7], upper mid = 7. If 7 is valid, left becomes 7; if invalid, right becomes 6. Both branches converge to the last valid candidate.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.lower_mid_retain: With adjacent candidates, lower-biased mid equals left and left = mid leaves both boundaries unchanged, causing a possible infinite loop.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.compute_upper_mid: Upper bias guarantees that retaining a valid midpoint with left = mid still advances left.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.keep_valid: A valid midpoint can be the maximum true candidate, so it remains while all smaller candidates become irrelevant.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.discard_invalid: True-to-false monotonicity proves an invalid midpoint and every larger candidate cannot be the last true answer.

items.prompt: Which postconditions together prove that x is the minimum feasible integer in the declared answer domain? Select all that apply.

options.text: Verify x lies inside the declared answer domain.
Verify x is the upper bound or feasible(x + 1) is false.
Verify x is the lower bound or feasible(x - 1) is false.
Verify feasible(x) is true.

feedback.reason: A minimum is proven by feasibility plus predecessor infeasibility or the domain boundary.

blocks.text: Feasibility and minimality are separate postconditions

To prove x is the minimum feasible integer, show it is a legal candidate, show it works, and show the immediately preceding legal integer does not work. Monotonicity then extends predecessor failure to every smaller candidate.

items: Range: x must lie inside the declared answer domain.
Feasibility: feasible(x) must be true, or x cannot be returned at all.
Minimality: either x is the lower endpoint or feasible(x - 1) is false.
The status of x + 1 is irrelevant to minimization; under false-to-true monotonicity it is normally true as well.

blocks.title: Example transition
blocks.text: If candidates 3, 4, 5 yield false, true, true, then x = 4 is in range, feasible(4) is true, and feasible(3) is false. Those facts prove 4 is the first feasible value.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.successor_infeasible: For a false-to-true predicate, a candidate after the minimum is normally feasible; successor infeasibility would contradict the assumed transition rather than prove minimality.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.check_range: A value outside the declared candidate domain cannot be the answer even if an accidentally callable predicate returns true.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.check_feasible: The requested result must satisfy every constraint encoded by the feasibility predicate.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.check_predecessor: Predecessor infeasibility, or the absence of a legal predecessor at the lower endpoint, proves no smaller candidate is feasible.

items.prompt: The integer answer domain contains W candidates and feasible(x) costs O(n). Select total time and the iterative outer search's own auxiliary space, excluding predicate workspace.
constraints: The outer search halves the answer range and stores only a constant number of scalar variables.

feedback.reason: Answer-space width determines predicate-call count, and input size determines each call's cost.

blocks.text: Multiply outer iterations by predicate work
Halving W >= 2 integer candidates takes O(log W) outer iterations. Each iteration evaluates feasible(mid) once, and the prompt gives that evaluation O(n) time.
Cost derivation

items: Predicate calls: O(log W).
Work per call: O(n).
Total time: O(log W) × O(n) = O(n log W).
The iterative outer loop stores only left, right, mid, and a constant number of results, so its own auxiliary space is O(1).

blocks.title: Scope of the space dimension
blocks.text: The question explicitly excludes predicate workspace. Whole-algorithm peak space would be O(1) plus whatever feasible(x) allocates.

items.prompt: A minimum-capacity search uses candidate range [maxJob, sumJobs], and each feasibility check scans n jobs. Select the standard time bound in terms of range width R = sumJobs - maxJob + 1.
constraints: Feasibility is false-to-true across the range.

feedback.reason: The search performs logarithmically many candidate checks, each scanning all jobs.

blocks.text: The logarithm uses numeric range width
The inclusive candidate interval [maxJob, sumJobs] contains R = sumJobs - maxJob + 1 integers. With R >= 2, halving that interval requires O(log R) feasibility evaluations.
Cost derivation

items: Candidate levels: O(log R).
One capacity check scans n jobs: O(n).
Total: O(log R) × O(n) = O(n log R).
The number of jobs controls predicate cost; the numeric difference between sumJobs and maxJob controls the number of candidate levels.

blocks.title: Do not replace R with n without proof
blocks.text: R can be much larger than n when job magnitudes are large. Complexity must retain log R unless the input contract supplies a relation that bounds R by a function of n.

items.prompt: A maximum-minimum-distance solver first sorts n positions, then each feasibility check scans them in O(n), and the answer range has width R. Select total time.
constraints: Comparison sorting costs O(n log n).
Binary search performs O(log R) feasibility checks.

time: O(n log n + n log R)
O(n log n + n log R)

time.sort_plus_search: O(n log n + n log R)

feedback.reason: Both preprocessing and answer-space search contribute to total cost.

blocks.text: Add sorting to all feasibility scans
The distance predicate needs positions in order, so comparison sorting is a one-time O(n log n) phase. The answer-space loop then performs O(log R) checks, each scanning all n positions.
Lifecycle derivation

items: Preprocessing: O(n log n).
Search evaluations: O(log R).
Work per evaluation: O(n), so search work is O(n log R).
Total: O(n log n + n log R).

blocks.title: Neither term universally absorbs the other
blocks.text: Without a stated relationship between n and R, sorting or answer-space search may dominate, so both terms must remain.

items.prompt: A recursive answer-space binary search uses O(log W) recursion depth. Each frame evaluates a predicate using O(n) temporary space, releases that workspace, and only then makes its recursive call. Select peak auxiliary space.
constraints: Each recursive frame retains O(1) scalar state while its child runs.
Predicate-local O(n) workspaces do not overlap across recursion levels.

feedback.reason: Peak memory combines one active predicate workspace with the recursion stack.

blocks.text: Count simultaneously live memory
Peak auxiliary space is not the sum of every allocation ever made. It is the maximum storage live at one moment. The prompt guarantees predicate workspaces do not overlap across recursion levels.
Peak-space derivation

items: The recursive boundary search retains O(log W) frames with O(1) scalar state each.
At the frame evaluating feasibility, one O(n) temporary workspace is live.
That workspace is released before the child call, so it is not multiplied by recursion depth.
Peak auxiliary space is therefore O(n) + O(log W) = O(n + log W).

blocks.title: Counterfactual
blocks.text: If each frame retained its O(n) predicate buffer while recursing, the buffers would overlap and the bound would instead be O(n log W). The lifetime premise is decisive.

items.prompt: A feasibility predicate performs O(n log n) work, and the answer range contains W integer candidates. Select total binary-search time.
constraints: The predicate is evaluated independently at each outer iteration.

feedback.reason: Binary search does not make an expensive predicate constant-time.

blocks.text: Substitute the real predicate cost
With W >= 2 candidates, the outer binary search performs O(log W) independent predicate calls. Each call repeats O(n log n) work under the prompt's contract.
Cost derivation

items: Outer iterations: O(log W).
Work per iteration: O(n log n).
Total: O(log W) × O(n log n) = O(n log n log W).
The O(n log n) work cannot be treated as one-time preprocessing because the prompt says it is performed independently at every iteration.

blocks.title: Reusable accounting rule
blocks.text: Separate reusable preprocessing from per-candidate evaluation. Add preprocessing once; multiply only work that is repeated for each searched candidate.
